Is maternal tissue overlying the conceptus and later fuses with the parietalis.
Is maternal endometrium lining the rest of the uterus.
Are maternal tissue.

stem: A 66-year-old smoker with chronic bronchitis has PaO2 58 mmHg and PaCO2 55 mmHg on room air. What is the principal mechanism of his hypoxemia?
options: Diffusion limitation across a thickened membrane
explanation: In COPD, obstructed airways with perfused alveoli cause low V/Q units (physiologic shunt), the main cause of hypoxemia and an increased A-a gradient; hypercapnia reflects alveolar hypoventilation. (First Aid — Respiratory: Hypoxemia and V/Q mismatch)
optionExplanations: Would not correct with oxygen and is typical of congenital cardiac defects or atelectasis.
Occurs in fibrosis, mainly during exercise.
Raises PaCO2 but the A-a gradient is wide in COPD, indicating V/Q mismatch.
Applies at altitude and has a normal A-a gradient.

stem: Which artery chiefly supplies the posterior and inferior parts of the thyroid lobes?
explanation: The inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk) supplies the posteroinferior lobes and the parathyroids and is closely related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve; the superior thyroid artery (external carotid) supplies the upper pole. (First Aid — Endocrine: Thyroid anatomy)
optionExplanations: Supplies the upper pole and anterior surface.
Is an inconsistent midline branch to the isthmus.
Supplies the tongue.
Supplies the pharynx and not the thyroid.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a solitary 2-cm thyroid nodule with normal TSH. What is the best next step in evaluation?
explanation: A solitary thyroid nodule with normal or high TSH should be sampled by fine-needle aspiration (guided by ultrasound features); a suppressed TSH prompts a radionuclide scan. (First Aid — Endocrine: Thyroid nodules and cancer)
optionExplanations: Is reserved for a suppressed TSH to detect a hot nodule.
Is not done before cytology.
Is used to follow up differentiated thyroid cancer after thyroidectomy.
Is not recommended as a diagnostic approach.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with lupus has fatigue and jaundice. Hemoglobin is 7 g/dL, reticulocytes are raised, blood film shows spherocytes and the direct Coombs test is positive with anti-IgG. Where does hemolysis predominantly occur?
options: In the bone marrow by ineffective erythropoiesis
In small vessels due to fibrin strands
explanation: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is IgG-mediated; macrophages in the spleen remove opsonized red cells or bite off membrane forming spherocytes, giving extravascular hemolysis and positive direct Coombs. Steroids are first line; splenectomy later. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia)
optionExplanations: Characterizes cold agglutinin hemolysis and ABO incompatibility.
Occurs in megaloblastic anemia and thalassemia.
Is not a mechanism of hemolysis.
Occurs in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes.

stem: A 40-year-old woman wakes with inability to close her left eye, tearing, loss of forehead wrinkling and deviation of her mouth to the right. What is the lesion?
options: Right upper motor neuron facial palsy
Left lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy)
explanation: A lower motor neuron (peripheral) lesion of the left facial nerve paralyses the entire ipsilateral face including forehead and orbicularis oculi, and the mouth deviates away from the lesion; UMN lesions spare the forehead. Bell's palsy is the commonest cause. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Facial nerve palsy)
optionExplanations: A UMN lesion spares the forehead and eye closure because of bilateral cortical innervation, but here the forehead is also paralysed.
Causes loss of facial sensation and jaw deviation.
Causes medial deviation of the eye with diplopia.
Causes ptosis and a down-and-out eye.

stem: A stab wound hemisects the right side of the spinal cord at T8. Which tract is responsible for the ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception below the lesion?
explanation: In Brown-Sequard syndrome, ipsilateral dorsal column loss (vibration, proprioception, fine touch) occurs below the lesion with ipsilateral UMN weakness and contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning 1-2 levels below the lesion. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Brown-Sequard syndrome)
optionExplanations: Carries pain and temperature, which are lost contralaterally.
Causes ipsilateral spastic paralysis, not sensory loss.
Carries crude touch, which is mostly preserved.
Carries unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum.

stem: Which structure does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
explanation: The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve and nine tendons (four FDS, four FDP, FPL). The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal, as do palmaris longus and the palmar cutaneous branch. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue: Carpal tunnel anatomy)
optionExplanations: Passes through the tunnel and is the structure compressed.
Passes through the tunnel in its own synovial sheath.
Pass through the tunnel with the superficialis tendons.
Pass through the tunnel in the common flexor sheath.

stem: Following a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus, a patient cannot abduct the arm beyond 15 degrees and has numbness over the lateral upper arm. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The axillary nerve (C5-C6) winds around the surgical neck of the humerus supplying deltoid and teres minor and the skin of the lateral arm (regimental badge area); injury weakens abduction from 15 to 90 degrees and external rotation. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue: Upper extremity nerve injuries)
optionExplanations: Injury impairs the first 15 degrees of abduction and external rotation, with no sensory loss over the deltoid.
Injury causes a winged scapula.
Injury causes wrist drop.
Injury causes weak elbow flexion and lateral forearm numbness.

stem: The tendon of which muscle lies in the groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid bone?
explanation: Peroneus longus passes behind the lateral malleolus, then runs in a groove on the cuboid across the sole to insert on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base, supporting the transverse and lateral arches and everting the foot. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue: Lower limb anatomy)
optionExplanations: Inserts onto the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal.
Inserts mainly onto the navicular tuberosity.
Passes under the sustentaculum tali to the distal phalanx of the great toe.
Inserts onto the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal.

stem: After a crush injury destroys the head of the talus, which foot structure is most impaired functionally?
options: Subtalar joint with no effect on the arches
explanation: The talar head forms the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch, receiving body weight and transferring it to the navicular, cuneiforms and medial three metatarsals; talar injury also risks avascular necrosis. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue: Foot arches and ankle anatomy)
optionExplanations: Has the cuboid as its keystone.
Depends on metatarsal heads.
Is controlled by gastrocnemius and soleus acting through the calcaneus.
The talar head directly participates in the medial arch.

stem: A wound swab grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. Which organism is it?
explanation: S. aureus is the coagulase-positive staphylococcus with golden colonies and protein A; it is the commonest cause of surgical site infections, abscesses, osteomyelitis and acute endocarditis. (First Aid — Microbiology: Gram-positive organisms)
optionExplanations: Is catalase-positive but coagulase-negative and novobiocin-sensitive.
Is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-resistant, causing UTIs in young women.
Forms chains and is catalase-negative.
Is catalase-negative and grows in bile and 6.5% NaCl.

stem: A 30-year-old man from Kashmir has a painless nodule on the forearm that has ulcerated centrally with a raised edge, with no pigmentation or systemic upset. A slit-skin smear shows amastigotes. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Old-world cutaneous leishmaniasis (L. tropica, L. major) is transmitted by sandflies; a chronic painless ulcer with a raised edge ('oriental sore') and amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) in macrophages confirms it. Treat with sodium stibogluconate or intralesional/local therapy. (First Aid — Microbiology: Protozoa — Leishmania)
optionExplanations: Features a painless ulcer with a black eschar and surrounding edema.
Features apple-jelly nodules from cutaneous tuberculosis and no amastigotes.
Causes an annular scaly lesion with a clear center.
Gives a pearly rolled-edge ulcer in older, sun-exposed skin.

stem: A patient has hepatocellular carcinoma complicating hepatitis B cirrhosis. Which is the most common extrahepatic site of metastasis?
explanation: HCC spreads by direct hepatic vein/portal vein invasion and hematogenously, with the lungs being the commonest extrahepatic site, followed by regional lymph nodes and bone. Alpha-fetoprotein is the tumor marker. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Liver tumors)
optionExplanations: Is a rare site of metastasis for HCC.
Is more typical for gastric (Krukenberg) or colorectal tumors.
Is unusual.
Is rarely involved by metastasis.

stem: A 28-year-old nurse has fatigue and jaundice for 1 week. Serology shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative and anti-HBc IgM positive. What is the interpretation?
options: Window period of acute hepatitis B
explanation: In acute hepatitis B the window period occurs after HBsAg has disappeared but before anti-HBs appears; anti-HBc IgM is the only positive marker and identifies recent infection. (First Aid — Microbiology: Hepatitis serologic markers)
optionExplanations: Has HBsAg positive for over 6 months with anti-HBc IgG.
Shows anti-HBs only, with no anti-HBc.
Shows anti-HBs and anti-HBc IgG with negative HBsAg.
Has HBsAg and HBeAg positive.

stem: A medical student has had the complete hepatitis B vaccine series and has no history of infection. Which serologic profile is expected?
options: HBsAg positive and anti-HBc IgM positive
Anti-HBs positive and anti-HBc IgG positive
HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative and anti-HBc IgG positive
Anti-HBs positive only, with HBsAg and anti-HBc negative
explanation: The vaccine contains recombinant HBsAg, so it induces only anti-HBs; anti-HBc is absent because there was no viral replication. (First Aid — Microbiology: Hepatitis B serology)
optionExplanations: Indicates acute infection.
Indicates recovery from natural infection.
Indicates isolated core antibody, e.g., low-level infection or window period.
Indicates high infectivity, not vaccination.

stem: A patient has low T4 and low TSH. After intravenous TRH, the TSH rises substantially and T4 later increases. At which level is the lesion?
options: Peripheral tissue resistance to thyroid hormone
explanation: A normal or exaggerated TSH response to TRH indicates healthy pituitary thyrotropes and a deficient TRH supply (hypothalamic disease), whereas absent response indicates pituitary failure. (First Aid — Endocrine: Hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis)
optionExplanations: Causes high TSH with low T4.
Would show no TSH response to TRH.
Causes high T4 and high or normal TSH.
Gives low total T4 with normal free T4 and TSH.

stem: Which chemical mediators released at the site of tissue injury directly activate and sensitize peripheral nociceptors, and whose synthesis is inhibited by NSAIDs?
options: Serotonin and dopamine in the dorsal root ganglion
explanation: Bradykinin activates nociceptors, while prostaglandins (PGE2) sensitize them to bradykinin and histamine; NSAIDs lower PG synthesis by inhibiting COX. (First Aid — Pathology: Inflammation mediators; Pharmacology: NSAIDs)
optionExplanations: Are T-cell cytokines for adaptive immunity, not primary nociceptor sensitizers.
Are central neurotransmitters, not tissue-injury mediators.
Are autonomic neurotransmitters.
Increase vascular permeability and chemotaxis, but are not the main nociceptor sensitizers inhibited by NSAIDs.

stem: Which factor is the most common predisposing condition for thoracic aortic dissection?
explanation: Chronic hypertension causes medial degeneration and is by far the commonest risk factor for aortic dissection; connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos), bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation and cocaine are other causes. (First Aid — Cardiovascular: Aortic dissection)
optionExplanations: Is an important cause in young patients but much less common overall.
Is an uncommon cause of aortitis and dissection.
Is a rare cause.
Is now a rare cause of aneurysm and not of dissection.

stem: A 19-year-old man has hyperextensible skin, joints that dislocate easily, easy bruising and poor wound healing with widened atrophic scars. What is the underlying defect?
options: A defect in collagen synthesis or structure
Deficiency of the enzyme lysyl oxidase due to copper deficiency
explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are inherited defects of collagen synthesis or processing (e.g., type V, type III in the vascular form, lysyl hydroxylase), causing hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints and tissue fragility, with risks of aortic and bowel rupture in the vascular type. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)
optionExplanations: Causes Marfan syndrome, with tall stature, lens subluxation and aortic dilatation.
Causes Menkes disease with kinky hair.
Is not the mechanism of Ehlers-Danlos.
Causes scurvy with perifollicular hemorrhages and bleeding gums.

stem: A child with hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycemia has blood tests drawn during an episode. Which combination is expected in von Gierke disease?
options: Hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia
Hypoglycemia with raised ketones and normal lactate
Hypoglycemia with hyperammonemia and low urea
Hypoglycemia with high insulin and C-peptide
explanation: In G6Pase deficiency, glucose-6-phosphate accumulates and is shunted to lactate (lactic acidosis), uric acid (via the pentose phosphate pathway and reduced renal excretion) and fat (hypertriglyceridemia), producing hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly and renomegaly. (First Aid — Biochemistry: Glycogen storage diseases)
optionExplanations: Is typical of ketotic hypoglycemia or MCAD deficiency.
Suggests a urea cycle defect.
Suggests adrenal insufficiency.
Suggests hyperinsulinism or insulinoma.

stem: A competent 60-year-old man with acute appendicitis refuses surgery after being fully informed of the risks, including death. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Respect his decision, document the informed refusal and continue to offer treatment
Operate under the principle of beneficence
Obtain consent from his adult son and proceed
explanation: Respect for autonomy means a competent adult with adequate information may refuse any treatment, even life-saving; document the discussion, ensure capacity, keep offering options and provide palliative or supportive care. (First Aid — Biostatistics, Epidemiology, Ethics, and Patient Safety: Autonomy and informed consent)
optionExplanations: Would violate autonomy, as a competent adult may refuse treatment.
Surrogate consent is only for patients lacking capacity.
Is not appropriate for a competent adult refusing treatment.
Refusing treatment does not itself indicate incapacity.

stem: A researcher measures exposure and outcome simultaneously in a sample of 2,000 people at one point in time to estimate the prevalence of hypertension. What is this study design?
explanation: A cross-sectional study assesses exposure and disease together at a single time, giving prevalence but not incidence or temporality, and is useful for planning health services. (First Aid — Biostatistics, Epidemiology, Ethics, and Patient Safety: Study designs)
optionExplanations: Follows exposed and unexposed groups over time to calculate incidence.
Starts with cases and controls and compares past exposure.
Assigns an intervention randomly to participants.
Describes a group of patients without a comparison group.

stem: A patient has an end-diastolic volume of 150 mL and an end-systolic volume of 75 mL. What is the ejection fraction?
explanation: Stroke volume = EDV - ESV = 150 - 75 = 75 mL; ejection fraction = SV/EDV = 75/150 = 50%. (First Aid — Cardiovascular: Cardiac output and ejection fraction)
optionExplanations: Would correspond to a stroke volume of about 37 mL (dilated failing ventricle).
Would require a stroke volume of 60 mL.
Confuses ESV with stroke volume.
Would mean the ventricle empties completely.

stem: Para-aminohippurate (PAH) is infused to measure renal plasma flow. Plasma PAH is 0.02 mg/mL, urine PAH is 10 mg/mL and urine flow is 1.2 mL/min. What is the effective renal plasma flow?
explanation: PAH is almost fully secreted and filtered, so its clearance estimates effective renal plasma flow: C = (U x V)/P = (10 x 1.2)/0.02 = 600 mL/min. (First Aid — Renal: Clearance and renal plasma flow)
optionExplanations: Corresponds to the typical GFR, not renal plasma flow.
Would arise from an arithmetic mistake in the clearance formula.
Is the renal blood flow range with hematocrit not applied properly.
Is the product of the urine concentration and flow divided incorrectly.

stem: A drug has a clearance of 5 L/h and a target steady-state plasma concentration of 10 mg/L. Its oral bioavailability is 50%. What maintenance dosing rate is required?
explanation: Maintenance dose rate = (CL x Css)/F = (5 x 10)/0.5 = 100 mg/h; for an IV infusion with F = 1, the rate would be 50 mg/h. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetics — maintenance dose)
optionExplanations: Ignores the bioavailability correction.
Multiplies by bioavailability instead of dividing.
Divides Css by CL instead of multiplying.
Misplaces a factor of ten in the calculation.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has a painless midline neck swelling just below the hyoid bone that rises when he protrudes his tongue and swallows. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The thyroglossal duct cyst is a remnant of the thyroglossal duct (foramen cecum to thyroid isthmus) and lies in the midline moving with swallowing and tongue protrusion; treat with Sistrunk procedure removing the central hyoid. (First Aid — Endocrine: Thyroid embryology)
optionExplanations: Presents as a lateral neck swelling along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
Presents in infancy as a soft transilluminating posterior triangle mass.
Lies in the midline but does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion.
Is mobile, tender and does not move with tongue protrusion.

stem: A plastic surgeon plans a pedicled transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous (TRAM) flap for breast reconstruction. Which vessel is the main blood supply to the flap?
explanation: A pedicled TRAM flap is based on the superior epigastric artery (continuation of the internal thoracic artery) running down the rectus abdominis muscle, anastomosing with the inferior epigastric artery. (First Aid — Anatomy: Abdominal wall vasculature)
optionExplanations: Is the pedicle of a free TRAM or DIEP flap, not a pedicled TRAM.
Supplies the lower lateral abdominal wall skin but is not the pedicle.
Supplies the lateral chest wall, not the rectus abdominis.
Supplies the iliacus and iliac crest region.

stem: A man has severe throat and ear pain on swallowing, loss of the gag reflex on the left and loss of sensation from the left tonsil and posterior one-third of the tongue. Which nerve is involved?
explanation: CN IX carries sensation from the tonsil, oropharynx, posterior tongue and middle ear (Jacobson's nerve), and is the afferent limb of the gag reflex, with CN X the efferent limb. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia presents with throat pain referred to the ear. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Cranial nerve IX)
optionExplanations: Supplies the anterior two-thirds of the tongue with taste and facial muscles, not tonsillar sensation.
Is purely motor to the tongue.
Supplies the general sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the lingual nerve.
Provides the efferent limb of the gag reflex but the afferent and tonsillar sensation is glossopharyngeal.

stem: A 62-year-old man undergoing a laparotomy for abdominal distension is found to have gelatinous mucinous material filling the peritoneal cavity arising from a ruptured appendiceal mucinous neoplasm. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is gelatinous mucinous ascites from peritoneal seeding of a low-grade appendiceal (or ovarian) mucinous neoplasm; management is cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Appendiceal tumors)
optionExplanations: Causes caseating granulomas and ascites with high ADA, not mucinous deposits.
Is ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion.
Is an asbestos-related tumor with peritoneal thickening.
Presents with flushing, diarrhea and right heart valve disease after hepatic metastases.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has an incidental 1-cm yellow nodule at the tip of the appendix after appendectomy. Histology shows nests of uniform neuroendocrine cells. Which test would be used if carcinoid syndrome were suspected?
explanation: The appendix is the commonest site of carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors, usually at the tip and benign when under 2 cm. Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, wheeze) occurs only with liver metastases and is diagnosed by raised urinary 5-HIAA, a serotonin metabolite. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Carcinoid tumors)
optionExplanations: Is used for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumors.
Is used for pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma.
Is used for pancreatic cancer.
Is used for colorectal cancer follow-up.

stem: The appendicular artery, which supplies the appendix and is ligated during appendectomy, is a branch of which artery?
explanation: The appendicular artery arises from the posterior caecal branch of the ileocolic artery (from the SMA) and is an end artery, so thrombosis in appendicitis leads to gangrene and perforation. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Blood supply of the gut)
optionExplanations: Supplies the ascending colon.
Supplies the transverse colon.
Supplies the hindgut.
Supplies the upper rectum.

stem: Section of a single posterior (dorsal) spinal nerve root would produce which deficit?
options: Loss of all sensory modalities in the corresponding dermatome with no motor loss
Flaccid paralysis of the corresponding myotome with intact sensation
Loss of pain and temperature only, with preserved touch
Complete loss of motor and sensory function in the limb
explanation: Dorsal roots carry afferent fibres with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion; interruption gives anesthesia in the dermatome (with overlap from adjacent roots making it partial) and loss of reflexes, but no motor deficit. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Spinal cord anatomy)
optionExplanations: Would result from ventral root damage.
Would suggest a spinothalamic or syrinx pattern.
Indicates upper motor neuron injury.
Indicates mixed spinal nerve or plexus injury.

stem: A patient has occlusion of one anterior cerebral artery distal to the anterior communicating artery. Which structure provides collateral supply to the affected territory from the opposite side?
explanation: The anterior communicating artery connects the two anterior cerebral arteries in the circle of Willis, allowing cross-flow if one ACA or the ICA is occluded; the posterior communicating artery links the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Circle of Willis)
optionExplanations: Connects the internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries.
Is an orbital branch of the internal carotid and not a cerebral collateral.
Supplies the posterior circulation.
Are end arteries of the MCA to deep structures with no collaterals.

stem: A 20-day-old term neonate has fever, tachypnea and grunting with lobar infiltrates on chest radiograph. Which organism is the most likely cause of pneumonia?
explanation: Neonatal pneumonia is most commonly due to group B Streptococcus (vertical transmission), with E. coli and Listeria as other pathogens; empirical therapy is ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside or cefotaxime. (First Aid — Microbiology: Neonatal infections)
optionExplanations: Is the commonest cause beyond 3 months of age.
Causes afebrile staccato cough in infants at 1 to 3 months.
Causes atypical pneumonia in school-aged children.
Occurs in immunocompromised infants such as those with HIV or SCID.

stem: A tall, thin 19-year-old smoker develops sudden right pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Chest radiograph shows absent peripheral lung markings on the right with a visible visceral pleural edge. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Rupture of apical subpleural blebs in tall thin young smokers causes spontaneous pneumothorax; radiograph shows a visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it. (First Aid — Respiratory: Pneumothorax)
optionExplanations: Usually has a normal radiograph or a peripheral wedge-shaped opacity.
Shows lobar consolidation rather than absent lung markings.
Shows a meniscus-shaped opacity with blunting of the costophrenic angle.
Does not cause loss of lung markings.

stem: A ventilated trauma patient suddenly becomes hypotensive and hypoxic with distended neck veins, absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation to the left. What is the immediate management?
options: Needle decompression of the right hemithorax
explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; the trachea deviates away from the affected side. Immediate needle decompression (second intercostal space midclavicular line or fifth space anterior axillary line) is followed by a chest drain. (First Aid — Respiratory: Tension pneumothorax)
optionExplanations: Delays life-saving treatment in a clinical diagnosis.
Treats tamponade, which presents with muffled heart sounds and equal breath sounds.
Does not relieve pleural pressure.
Does not correct the obstructive cause.

stem: A thoracocentesis needle is to be inserted for a large pleural effusion. Where should it be placed to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle?
options: Just below the lower border of the upper rib
Immediately along the midline of the intercostal space
Just above the upper border of the lower rib of the intercostal space
Through the lower border of the rib above
explanation: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN) lie in the costal groove under the lower border of each rib, so the needle is inserted just above the rib below; layers pierced are skin, fasciae, intercostal muscles, endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura. (First Aid — Respiratory: Thoracic anatomy)
optionExplanations: Places the needle in the costal groove containing the vein, artery and nerve.
Risks collateral branches of the neurovascular bundle.
Would encounter dense tissue.
Would hit the bundle.

stem: Which ECG finding is most common in acute pulmonary embolism?
explanation: Sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG abnormality in PE (and T-wave inversions in V1-V4); S1Q3T3, right axis deviation and RBBB occur less commonly. (First Aid — Cardiovascular/Respiratory: Pulmonary embolism)
optionExplanations: Is classic but found in a minority of patients.
Is less frequent.
Suggests acute pericarditis.
Is not characteristic of PE.

stem: A man stabbed in the chest has hypotension, distended jugular veins and muffled heart sounds. Which type of shock is this?
explanation: Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) indicates cardiac tamponade, an obstructive shock with reduced preload; pulsus paradoxus and electrical alternans may be present. Treat with pericardiocentesis. (First Aid — Cardiovascular: Cardiac tamponade)
optionExplanations: Presents with flat neck veins.
Presents with pulmonary edema and displaced apex.
Presents with warm skin and bradycardia.
Presents with urticaria and bronchospasm.

stem: A house-fire victim has lactic acidosis, normal PaO2 and cherry-red skin; cyanide poisoning is suspected. Which type of hypoxia and mechanism are present?
options: Hypoxic hypoxia from low inspired oxygen
Stagnant hypoxia from low cardiac output
Histotoxic hypoxia from inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV)
explanation: Cyanide binds the ferric iron of cytochrome oxidase (complex IV), halting oxidative phosphorylation: oxygen cannot be used despite normal delivery, causing lactic acidosis. Treat with hydroxocobalamin, sodium thiosulfate or nitrites. (First Aid — Biochemistry: Electron transport chain inhibitors)
optionExplanations: Is the mechanism of carbon monoxide poisoning.
Has a low PaO2.
Results from reduced blood flow.
Gives chocolate-brown blood with a normal PaO2, treated with methylene blue.

stem: A patient with hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy has carpopedal spasm and perioral numbness. Which ECG change is expected?
explanation: Hypocalcemia prolongs the ST segment and QT interval by delaying repolarization, with tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs; severe cases cause torsades. (First Aid — Endocrine/Renal: Hypocalcemia)
optionExplanations: Occur in hyperkalemia.
Occurs in hypercalcemia.
Occur in hypokalemia.
Is seen in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

stem: In global cerebral hypoxia-ischemia (e.g., after cardiac arrest), which neurons are most selectively vulnerable?
options: Anterior horn motor neurons of the spinal cord
Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra
Pyramidal neurons of the hippocampal CA1 region
explanation: Neurons of the hippocampus (CA1 Sommer sector), neocortex (layers 3, 5, 6) and cerebellar Purkinje cells are most vulnerable to hypoxia; red neurons appear 12-24 hours after the insult. Watershed zones are also at risk. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Ischemic brain disease)
optionExplanations: Are relatively resistant to global ischemia.
Are lost in Parkinson disease, not primarily from ischemia.
Are glial cells and not the most vulnerable.
Are glial cells lining the ventricles and are resistant.

stem: A malnourished patient who has had no food for 3 days is started on aggressive enteral feeding. Two days later she develops weakness, arrhythmias and respiratory failure. Which electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark of this syndrome?
explanation: Refeeding syndrome follows insulin-driven intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium when carbohydrates are reintroduced, causing hypophosphatemia (hallmark), hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, thiamine deficiency, arrhythmias and respiratory muscle failure. (First Aid — Renal: Electrolyte disturbances / Nutrition)
optionExplanations: Occurs in renal failure and tumor lysis.
Is not a feature of refeeding.
Is not characteristic of refeeding.
Is not characteristic; hypomagnesemia accompanies refeeding.

stem: During leukocyte extravasation, which molecule mediates transmigration (diapedesis) of neutrophils between endothelial cells?
explanation: Neutrophil extravasation proceeds through rolling (selectins), activation (chemokines), tight binding (integrins with ICAM-1) and transmigration through endothelial junctions via PECAM-1 (CD31) before chemotaxis to the site. (First Aid — Immunology/Pathology: Leukocyte extravasation)
optionExplanations: Mediates rolling, not firm adhesion or transmigration.
Mediates firm adhesion.
Is the selectin ligand on leukocytes for rolling.
Is an extracellular matrix glycoprotein.

stem: Histamine, released from mast cells in allergic reactions, is formed from which amino acid by decarboxylation?
explanation: Histidine decarboxylase converts histidine to histamine (vitamin B6-dependent); mast cell and basophil histamine causes vasodilation, bronchoconstriction and itching via H1 receptors. (First Aid — Biochemistry: Amino acid derivatives)
optionExplanations: Is the precursor of catecholamines and thyroid hormones.
Is the precursor of serotonin and niacin.
Is decarboxylated to GABA.
Is the precursor of nitric oxide and urea cycle intermediates.

stem: An 80-year-old man on warfarin who fell a week ago has progressive confusion. CT shows a crescent-shaped hypodense collection that crosses suture lines. Which is the diagnosis?
explanation: Subdural hematoma results from tearing of bridging veins, producing a crescent-shaped collection crossing sutures but not the falx; chronic collections appear hypodense in elderly or anticoagulated patients. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Intracranial hemorrhage)
optionExplanations: Is lens-shaped, does not cross sutures and follows arterial bleeding.
Shows blood in the sulci and basal cisterns.
Shows a parenchymal hyperdensity.
Shows punctate white-matter hemorrhages with a normal CT often.

stem: Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid arises from parafollicular C cells. Which hormone is a characteristic tumor marker?
explanation: Medullary thyroid cancer secretes calcitonin and shows amyloid stroma; it is associated with MEN2A and MEN2B (RET proto-oncogene). (First Aid — Endocrine: Thyroid cancer)
optionExplanations: Is a marker for follicular and papillary carcinoma after thyroidectomy.
Is secreted by the parathyroid chief cells.
Is produced by follicular cells.
Is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumors.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with exophthalmos, diffuse goiter and weight loss has thyroid function tests drawn. Which result pattern is expected in Graves disease?
options: High TSH with low free T4
High TSH with high free T4
Low TSH with low free T4
Normal TSH with high total T4 only
Low TSH with high free T4 and T3
explanation: In Graves disease, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate TSH receptors, increasing thyroid hormone and suppressing TSH through negative feedback; features include diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy and pretibial myxedema. (First Aid — Endocrine: Graves disease)
optionExplanations: Occurs in primary hypothyroidism.
Occurs in TSH-secreting adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance.
Occurs in central hypothyroidism.
Occurs when binding globulin is increased, e.g., in pregnancy.

stem: A 60-year-old smoker with small cell lung cancer has proximal leg weakness that improves with repeated effort, a dry mouth and hyporeflexia. Antibodies are directed against which target?
explanation: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release; strength improves with repeated use, autonomic dysfunction is common and it is paraneoplastic with small cell carcinoma. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Lambert-Eaton syndrome)
optionExplanations: Are targeted in myasthenia gravis, which worsens with activity.
Is a target in a variant of myasthenia gravis.
Is not a target of autoantibodies.
Are not the target in this disorder.

stem: At 35 weeks' gestation, which organ is the main source of estrogen (estriol) production in the maternal circulation?
explanation: Estriol in pregnancy is made by the placenta from fetal adrenal DHEA-S (fetoplacental unit); the corpus luteum supports early pregnancy until the placenta takes over at 8-10 weeks. (First Aid — Reproductive: Pregnancy hormones)
optionExplanations: Produces most estrogen before the placenta takes over.
Contributes little to the pregnancy estrogen rise.
Secretes trophic hormones, not estrogen.
Dominates in the first 8 weeks only.

stem: Which group of structures lies posterior to the first part of the duodenum?
options: Head of the pancreas and superior mesenteric vein only
Gastroduodenal artery, common bile duct and portal vein
Left renal vein and inferior vena cava
Inferior mesenteric vein and left colic artery
explanation: The first part of the duodenum lies posteriorly in contact with the gastroduodenal artery, the common bile duct and the portal vein, and the IVC beyond; this explains bleeding from posterior ulcers. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Duodenum anatomy)
optionExplanations: Lie behind the second and third parts, not these.
Lie behind the third part of the duodenum.
Lie in the retroperitoneum to the left, unrelated.
Lie behind the second part of the duodenum.

stem: A scuba diver surfaces rapidly and develops joint pain and chest tightness. Which gas forms bubbles in tissues to cause decompression sickness?
explanation: According to Henry's law, more nitrogen dissolves in tissues at high pressure; rapid ascent releases it as bubbles, causing joint pain, neurologic deficits and arterial gas embolism. Treat with 100% oxygen and hyperbaric recompression. (First Aid — Respiratory: Physiology under pressure)
optionExplanations: Is consumed by metabolism and does not form persistent bubbles.
Is highly soluble and transported as bicarbonate.
Is used in deep-diving mixtures and is less soluble than nitrogen.
Binds hemoglobin but does not form bubbles.

stem: A horseshoe kidney is fused across the midline at the lower poles and found lower than normal. Ascent during development was arrested by which structure?
explanation: In horseshoe kidney, the fused isthmus is trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery as the kidneys ascend, leaving the organ low; it is associated with Turner syndrome and increased risk of stones and infection. (First Aid — Renal: Horseshoe kidney)
optionExplanations: Lies higher and does not limit renal ascent.
Is at T12 and is not an obstruction.
Arises from the aorta and does not arrest ascent.
Does not limit the ascent of the kidney.

stem: The inferior suprarenal (adrenal) artery is a branch of which vessel?
explanation: Each adrenal gland has three arteries: superior (from inferior phrenic), middle (from abdominal aorta) and inferior (from renal artery); a single vein drains each gland (the left to the left renal vein, the right to the IVC). (First Aid — Endocrine: Adrenal anatomy)
optionExplanations: Gives the superior suprarenal arteries.
Gives the middle suprarenal artery directly.
Does not supply the adrenal.
Does not supply the adrenal.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent hemarthrosis and prolonged aPTT with normal PT and bleeding time. Factor IX activity is low. What is the diagnosis and its inheritance?
explanation: Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) is X-linked recessive factor IX deficiency with prolonged aPTT, normal PT and bleeding time and hemarthroses; treated with factor IX concentrates. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Coagulation disorders)
optionExplanations: Is due to factor VIII deficiency.
Has prolonged bleeding time and mucosal bleeding.
Is mild and not typically associated with hemarthrosis.
Features platelet function defects with prolonged bleeding time.

stem: Which is the best screening test for open neural tube defects at 16-18 weeks' gestation?
options: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein with a detailed ultrasound
explanation: Maternal serum AFP is raised in open neural tube defects and abdominal wall defects (low in Down syndrome); confirmation is by detailed ultrasound and amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase. Folic acid prevents NTD. (First Aid — Reproductive: Prenatal screening)
optionExplanations: Is elevated in Down syndrome and molar pregnancy.
Is low in Down syndrome.
Detects chromosomal abnormalities, not specific for NTD screening.
Assesses fetal well-being in late pregnancy.

stem: A 16-year-old girl with short stature, webbed neck and primary amenorrhea has streak ovaries. Which karyotype is most likely?
explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes streak gonads, short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, coarctation, horseshoe kidney and primary amenorrhea with high FSH. (First Aid — Reproductive: Turner syndrome)
optionExplanations: Is Klinefelter syndrome.
Is triple X with usually normal fertility.
Causes androgen insensitivity with a blind vagina and normal breasts, but no webbed neck.
Is Down syndrome.

stem: A surgeon dividing the peritoneal fold between the spleen and the left kidney during splenectomy must protect the tail of the pancreas. Which ligament is this?
explanation: The lienorenal ligament carries the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas between spleen and left kidney; careless dissection during splenectomy can cause pancreatic fistula. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Peritoneal ligaments)
optionExplanations: Contains the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.
Connects the stomach to the transverse colon.
Supports the splenic flexure.
Contains the portal triad.

stem: A patient with peptic ulcer disease takes aluminium hydroxide antacid. Which adverse effects are characteristic?
explanation: Aluminium hydroxide causes constipation, hypophosphatemia (binds phosphate), hypocalcemia and osteodystrophy in chronic use; magnesium hydroxide causes diarrhea and calcium carbonate may cause hypercalcemia and rebound acid secretion. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Antacids)
optionExplanations: Occur with magnesium hydroxide.
Occur with calcium carbonate (milk-alkali syndrome).
Are not features of aluminium antacids.
Are not features of aluminium antacids.

stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing gastroesophageal reflux has biopsy-proven Barrett esophagus. Which malignancy is he at increased risk of?
explanation: Chronic reflux causes metaplasia of the distal esophageal squamous epithelium into intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells (Barrett), predisposing to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Esophageal pathology)
optionExplanations: Is associated with alcohol, smoking, achalasia and caustic ingestion.
Is associated with H. pylori and nitrosamines.
Is a rare mesenchymal tumor.
Is a rare esophageal tumor, not linked to reflux.

stem: After a blow to the shoulder, a boxer cannot flex his elbow against resistance and has weak supination, with numbness over the lateral forearm. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7) supplies biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis, causing weak elbow flexion and supination when injured, with loss of sensation over the lateral forearm (lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve). (First Aid — Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue: Upper extremity nerve injuries)
optionExplanations: Injury causes wrist drop and weak extension, with brachioradialis being spared in flexion.
Injury causes deltoid weakness.
Injury causes weak pronation and thumb opposition.
Injury causes claw hand.

stem: Which hormone initiates the migrating motor complex of the small bowel during fasting?
explanation: Motilin, released from M cells of the duodenum every 90-120 minutes during fasting, initiates the migrating motor complex ('housekeeper' wave); erythromycin is a motilin receptor agonist. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: GI hormones)
optionExplanations: Stimulates acid secretion and gastric motility after meals.
Contracts the gallbladder and slows gastric emptying postprandially.
Stimulates bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas.
Inhibits GI secretions and motility.

stem: After a deep posterior knee laceration, a patient holds the foot dorsiflexed and everted, cannot plantarflex or invert it, and has sensory loss over the sole. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The tibial nerve supplies the plantar flexors and invertors (gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior, toe flexors) and the sole; its loss leaves dorsiflexors and evertors unopposed ('calcaneovalgus' posture). (First Aid — Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue: Lower extremity nerve injuries)
optionExplanations: Injury causes footdrop with plantarflexion and inversion, and sensory loss on the dorsum.
Injury causes footdrop with sensory loss in the first web space.
Injury causes weak eversion with sensory loss on the lateral lower leg and dorsum.
Is a purely sensory nerve of the lateral foot.
